'''''Rohdea japonica''''' is a species of plant native to [[Japan]], [[China]] and [[Korea]].<ref name="marcia">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=286777 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>Tanaka, N. (2010). A taxonomic revision of the genus ''Rohdea'' (Asparagaceae). Makinoa , n.s., 9: 1-54.</ref><ref>Ohwi, J. (1984). Flora of Japan (in English): 1-1067. Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.</ref><ref>Lee, W.T. (1996). Lineamenta Florae Koreae: 1-1688. Soul T'ukpyolsi: Ak'ademi Sojok.</ref> Common names include '''Nippon lily''', '''sacred lily''', and '''Japanese sacred lily.'''

It is a [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]], with [[fibrous roots]]. The [[leaf|leaves]] are [[evergreen]], broad lanceolate, 15–50 cm long and 2.5–7 cm broad, with an acute apex. The [[flower]]s are produced in a short, stout, dense spike 3–4 cm long, each flower pale yellowish, 4–5 mm long. This is a rare instance of pollination by snails.{{cn|date=August 2025}} The [[fruit]] is a red [[Berry (botany)|berry]] 8 mm diameter, produced in a tight cluster of several together.

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Kinka Ikenobo 錦花池坊 002.jpg|thumb|left|Traditional arrangement of ''Kinka [[Ikenobō]]'' school using ''omoto'' (''Rohdea japonica'')]]
It is cultivated as an ornamental plant. In [[Chinese language|Chinese]] it is called ''wan nian qing'' (simplified: [[wiktionary:万|万]][[wiktionary:年|年]][[wiktionary:青|青]]; traditional: 萬年青; <!--need pinyin-->lit. "evergreen"), and for this reason has been used symbolically in visual culture (e.g. on [http://www.maozhang.net/flowers/4585836984 Mao badges] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140813195533/http://www.maozhang.net/flowers/4585836984 |date=2014-08-13 }}). In [[Japanese language|Japanese]] it is called ''omoto''.

The plant is also used in [[traditional Chinese medicine]], though it is generally regarded as inedible and possibly toxic.
